content.title: WHY YOUR HEALTHY MEALS AREN'T {{WORKING}}
facts: **Broccoli** – Boiling it destroys most of its sulforaphane; steam it for 3-4 minutes instead to keep the compound intact.
**Olive oil** – Cooking it at high heat past its smoke point breaks it down into harmful compounds; save extra virgin for low heat or drizzling raw.
**Tomato sauce** – Skipping the oil means you absorb almost none of the lycopene; add 1 tbsp olive oil while simmering to actually absorb it.
**Chicken breast** – Cutting it right after cooking lets all the juices run out onto the board; rest it for 5-10 minutes first.
**Rice** – Cooking and serving it fresh spikes blood sugar hardest; cooling it in the fridge for a few hours creates resistant starch that blunts the spike.
**Spinach** – Eating it raw in huge amounts blocks iron and calcium absorption due to oxalates; a quick light sauté lowers that effect.
**Turmeric** – Sprinkling it on food alone barely gets absorbed; pair it with black pepper and a bit of fat to multiply absorption.

caption:
Small prep mistakes quietly cancel out a lot of the effort you put into eating well. Take broccoli: boiling pulls sulforaphane, its main anti-inflammatory compound, straight into the water, which is why steaming for just a few minutes protects it so much better. Olive oil is another sneaky one — heating it past its smoke point actually oxidizes the healthy fats into compounds your body has to work harder to deal with, so it's smarter to save it for finishing a dish rather than frying. And tomato sauce without any oil means the lycopene inside stays locked in the cell walls; that little splash of olive oil while it simmers is what actually unlocks it into a form your body can use. Everyone's kitchen habits are different, so start with whichever one feels easiest to fix first.
